title: Rabbi Yehuda Gelustra
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: In Berakhot 22a they said: When Rav Dimi came, he said, "Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda Gelusetra said," etc. From this it appears that he was his colleague or lived in the generation of Rabbi Akiva. But in Yuchasin he cites a different reading, as follows: "When Rav Dimi came he said, Rav Yehuda Kelusterah and Rabbi Akiva said, and it appears that they were students of Rabbi Yochanan," end quote. And in Dikdukei Soferim (דק״ס) he reads "Rabbi Yehuda Kelastarah." But according to all the readings, Hyman does not find anywhere else a tanna or amora with such a name, nor does he find an amora named Akiva who was a student of Rabbi Yochanan. By a conjecture close to the truth, Hyman proposes that the word "gelusetra" is as we find in Shabbat 124a: "a door bolt that has a knob at its head," and Rav Dimi's intention was to say that Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda said one thing: that a sick person who has had a voluntary emission requires forty se'ah.

notes.text: Gelustra denotes the knob on the door bolt mentioned in Shabbat 124a. Hyman proposes treating the word as an ordinary noun rather than part of a sage’s name; Kelustera and Kelastara are recorded variants.
The checked Berakhot 22a passage contrasts a sick man’s involuntary emission with חולה המרגיל, a voluntary emission.

Berakhot 22a directly gives Yehudah Gelostra and the contrast between a sick person’s involuntary and voluntary emission. Hyman’s near-the-truth conjecture that gelustra is an ordinary noun, and his Yuchasin/Dikdukei Soferim variants and absence argument, remain attributed to him rather than newly established by a bounded search.
